title: Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram
hook: love and Shiva are two, say those who don't know: Tirumular's short verse

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram: Kannappa, the hunter who knew none of the rules and was stopped by Shiva's own hand. Did you give one thing as it is, without waiting for perfect? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-five.

Love and Shiva are two, say those who don't know. That's the first line of a short verse in Tamil, and it's spoken by a man the tradition calls Tirumular. The story of how he got that name is strange. A traveling yogi comes upon a herd of cows in a field, gathered around the body of their cowherd, who has just died. The cows are lowing, circling, refusing to leave him. The yogi can't bear it. So, the story says, he leaves his own body and enters the cowherd's. And the cowherd stands up. Today, the last of our Tamil days, and a man who came back to life for the sake of some cows.
screen: `COWS AROUND A DEAD COWHERD.` → `A YOGI CAN'T BEAR IT.` → `THE COWHERD STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the rest of the story, as the Periya Puranam tells it, in paraphrase. The cows, comforted, go home. The yogi means to return to his own body afterward, but when he looks for it, it's gone. Shiva's will, the story says. So he stays in the cowherd's body, under the cowherd's name, Mular, and settles down to meditate and compose the Tirumantiram, a long book of verses on Shiva and the path to him. That book sits in the Tirumurai, the same sacred collection that holds the Tevaram. Now the verse from the hook, in paraphrase. Love and Shiva are two, say those who don't know. No one knows that love itself is Shiva. When they know that love itself is Shiva, they rest there, as love, as Shiva. Turn it once. The verse doesn't say Shiva is loving, the way you'd say a person is kind. It goes further. It says the love is Shiva. Not a quality he has, but who he is. Turn it again, and go back to the field. The whole story starts with a man who couldn't bear the grief of some cows. He wasn't seeking a vision. He was moved by animals crying for their herder, and he gave up his own body to comfort them. Before he wrote a single verse, he'd already done what the verse says. And once more, looking back over these days in the Tamil south. Appar, who belonged so wholly to Shiva that a king couldn't summon him. Sambandar, whose heart was stolen. Kannappa, who held nothing back. And a cowherd who was really a yogi, saying it plainly: love itself is Shiva.
screen: `THE BODY HE COULDN'T FIND` · `THE TIRUMANTIRAM` · `LOVE ITSELF IS SHIVA` · `HE DID IT BEFORE HE WROTE IT`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the love itself. Sit, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind someone you love, a person or even an animal. See their face for a moment, and feel the warmth that comes with it. Now, gently, let the face fade, and stay with the warmth. Not the person now, just the love. Breathe there. When the mind goes looking for the face again, let it, and then come back to the warmth. If you pray, you can rest in the verse's words: love itself is Shiva. The bell holds the time.
Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram. Today, Tirumular, the yogi who entered a cowherd's body to comfort his cows, and whose verse says love itself is Shiva. Today's word.
screen: `TAMIL SHAIVISM AND THE TEVARAM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Tamil Shaivism and the Tevaram. Today, when someone's distress catches you, let yourself be moved, and do one small thing about it. Tomorrow, we travel north and east, to Bengal. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-five.

screen: `DAY 1375 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BENGAL'S SHAKTA AND VAISHNAVA STREAMS.`

howItsDone: Tirumular is honored among the Nayanmars, the Shaiva saints of the Tamil country, and the words 'anbe sivam', love is Shiva, from his verse are spoken and written by Tamil Shaivas.

notes: Editor pass: the writer's draft retold Sundarar's interrupted wedding and the 'madman' hymn, already told on day 1371. Rewritten as a new angle on the same index line: Tirumular and the 'anbe sivam' verse. New practice and carry; the look-back now names this run's figures (Appar, Sambandar, Kannappa, Tirumular).
The verse number varies by edition (often given as 270); the script cites it by first line only. Confirm paraphrase.

The traditional claim that he wrote one verse a year over thousands of years is deliberately left out under the claims rule. The yogi's origin (Kailasa, Sundaranatha) and the village (Sattanur) are left unnamed.
The Tirumantiram is the tenth Tirumurai, not part of the Tevaram (1–7); the script says only 'in the Tirumurai, the same collection'. Confirm.
